questions.stem: Mr Pascoe, a 63-year-old electrician seen in general practice, has 6 weeks of right neck pain spreading to his lateral forearm and thumb, with tingling in his thumb and index finger. Before testing power, you want a provocation test that supports compression of a right cervical nerve root in its foramen. Which manoeuvre should you perform?
options: Flex the neck fully forward and ask about electric shocks down the spine or into the limbs
Hold both wrists fully flexed for 60 seconds and ask about tingling in the hand
Extend the neck, rotate and side-bend it to the right, then press gently down on the head
Flex the shoulder to 90 degrees, internally rotate it and ask about pain at the shoulder
questions.why: This is Spurling's test. Extending, rotating and side-bending the neck towards the painful side narrows that foramen, and adding axial load reproduces the radicular pain down the arm. It is specific for cervical radiculopathy. Avoid it if there has been trauma or the neck may be unstable.
notes: This is Lhermitte's sign, which suggests disease of the cord (myelopathy or demyelination) rather than compression of a nerve root in its foramen.
This is Phalen's test for carpal tunnel syndrome. It does not explain neck pain, pain radiating from the shoulder or weakness above the wrist.
This is the Hawkins-Kennedy test for subacromial impingement, a shoulder problem. It does not stress the cervical foramen.

questions.stem: Mr Pascoe, 63, comes back to his GP 10 days later. His right shoulder abduction and elbow flexion are 4/5 and stable, his right biceps reflex is reduced, and he has no upper motor neuron signs. MRI shows right C4-5 and C5-6 foraminal stenosis with a normal cord. His pain is 4/10 on paracetamol. What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Analgesia, physiotherapy, modified duties and a non-urgent spinal surgical referral
Same-day transfer to the emergency department for urgent decompressive surgery
Analgesia and physiotherapy only, with GP review if the pain persists beyond 6 months
Regular slow-release oxycodone, strict bed rest and a soft cervical collar
questions.why: Most cervical radiculopathy settles with conservative care. Even so, an objective motor deficit with a concordant MRI warrants routine referral to a spinal surgeon. Progressive weakness or signs of myelopathy would make the referral urgent.
notes: He has no myelopathy, his cord is normal and his weakness is stable. Emergency decompression is for cord compression or rapidly progressive weakness.
A persisting motor deficit with concordant root compression on MRI warrants specialist input. A plan that only reviews pain misses the weakness.
Opioids are not recommended for routine use in radiculopathy, and bed rest and collars delay recovery. He should stay active.

questions.stem: Mr Pascoe, 63, finds that his right arm pain eases when he rests his right hand on top of his head. His MRI shows right C5-6 foraminal stenosis compressing the right C6 nerve root, with a normal spinal cord. What best explains why this posture relieves his pain?
options: It relaxes the supraspinatus, easing impingement of its tendon under the acromion
Elevating the arm widens the costoclavicular space around the brachial plexus
Raising the arm flexes the neck, which widens the canal around the spinal cord
Shoulder abduction slackens the plexus and lowers tension on the compressed root
questions.why: This is the shoulder abduction relief sign. Raising the arm shortens the path from the foramen to the limb, which reduces traction and tension on the compressed nerve root and so eases radicular pain. It points to radiculopathy rather than a shoulder problem.
notes: Raising the arm overhead makes subacromial impingement worse, not better. His pain also runs below the elbow to the thumb, which a rotator cuff problem would not explain.
Raising the arm narrows the costoclavicular space. That is why arm elevation brings on thoracic outlet symptoms rather than relieving them.
Resting the hand on the head does not meaningfully flex the neck. His cord is also normal, so canal space is not the cause of his pain.

questions.stem: Mr Pascoe, 63, has an MRI of his cervical spine for right arm radicular pain. It reports severe narrowing of the right intervertebral foramen at C5-6, between the C5 and C6 vertebrae. Which nerve root leaves the spinal canal through this foramen?
options: C5 root, since cervical roots exit below the pedicle of their numbered vertebra
C6 root, since cervical roots exit above the pedicle of their numbered vertebra
C7 root, since the root passes the disc and exits at the foramen one level down
C4 root, since roots exit one level above the cord segment they arise from
questions.why: There are 8 cervical roots but only 7 cervical vertebrae. Each cervical root exits above the vertebra of the same number, so the C6 root leaves at C5-6 and C8 leaves at C7-T1. From T1 downwards, roots exit below their vertebra.
notes: Exiting below the numbered vertebra is the thoracic and lumbar pattern. The C5 root exits at C4-5, which is where his moderate stenosis is.
A root that passes the disc and exits a level lower is how a lumbar disc affects the traversing root. A foraminal lesion in the neck compresses the root that exits at that level.
Roots are named for the foramen they exit through, not for a mismatch with cord segments. The C4 root exits at C3-4.
